title: Can One Word Become the Other?

concept.title: What the two allowed operations keep
body: You may (1) **swap any two letters** of a word, so the order of the letters is free, and (2) **exchange two existing letters** everywhere (all `a` become `b` and all `b` become `a`), which can move a count from one letter to another. Think about what these operations cannot change: the **set of letters used**, and the **multiset of counts** (for example "two letters occur 3 times, one letter occurs once").

body.code:
same_letters = set(a) == set(b)
same_counts = sorted(counts(a).values()) == sorted(counts(b).values())
answer = same_letters and same_counts

body: Operation 2 can never introduce a new letter, so the sets must be equal. It can reassign counts between letters, so only the sorted list of counts matters. If both conditions hold, you can always transform one word into the other.

statement: You can change a word with two operations, as often as you like. (1) Swap any two letters of the word. (2) Choose two letters that both occur in the word and exchange them everywhere (every `a` becomes `b` and every `b` becomes `a`). Print `yes` if the first word can be turned into the second word, otherwise `no`.
inputFormat: The first line has the first word.
The second line has the second word.

examples.note: Both words use a, b and c with the counts 1, 2 and 3 in some order, so exchanges and swaps can turn one into the other.
Counts 2 and 1 can be exchanged: yes.

hints: The words must have the same length and use the same set of letters.
The multiset of the counts of the letters must be the same.
Compare the sorted lists of counts.
